title: application-nagle-and-async-flush-interaction-lab-mar-2026
content:
Summary:
Quick lab notes exploring interaction between application-level async flush cadence (what client or server runtime does when it flushes application buffers) and TCP-level coalescing/Nagle (TCP_NODELAY on/off). We observed non-obvious tail latency amplification for small tokenized chunks when a proxy sits between client and runtime. Goal is to capture hypotheses, experiment matrix, raw observations, and recommended mitigations to try in staging.

Background / motivation:
- Many LLM streaming clients write small token fragments (8-64 bytes) and rely on the stack to push them out. On the server side the runtime may batch model tokens into ~1–4 token writes and call flush.
- TCP Nagle (coalescing) + delayed ACKs can cause extra RTT waits when small writes are sent; most services opt for TCP_NODELAY to avoid this.
- However, when there is a proxy (edge HTTP/gRPC proxy) in the middle that performs its own buffering or re-framing, the effective flush semantics change and can reintroduce waiting even when TCP_NODELAY is set on the runtime socket.
- We suspect interactions between (a) application flush cadence, (b) proxy chunking/buffering policy, and (c) delayed ACK/Nagle lead to p99 amplification in token latency under certain request patterns.

Hypotheses:
1) With small token writes and infrequent flush (server waits to accumulate n tokens or ms), enabling TCP_NODELAY at the runtime reduces mean but not necessarily p99 if the proxy coalesces.
2) gRPC (HTTP/2) with DATA frames and WINDOW updates may behave differently than HTTP/1.1 chunked responses when proxies do per-connection coalescing.
3) Deliberately aligning application flush cadence to proxy flush boundaries (or using explicit flush markers) reduces tail latency.
4) For cold KV-cache warmup (first completion after model start), extra latency effects are multiplicative because token generation time + networking waits stack.

Experiment matrix (staged tests):
- Clients: synthetic streaming client (python requests+threaded writer) and real SDK client (node-js streaming).
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 chunked vs HTTP/2 (gRPC-style streaming).
- Proxy: none (direct), edge-proxy with buffering enabled, edge-proxy with passthrough (no buffering).
- TCP_NODELAY: on/off on runtime backend socket.
- Server flush cadence: immediate flush (every token), grouped-2 (flush every 2 tokens), grouped-4, grouped-100ms timer (flush every 100ms regardless).
- Payloads: short tokens (avg 14B), medium (avg 50B), long fragments (avg 200B).
- KV cache state: warm (after 10 requests), cold (first request after idle).

Notes on setup:
- Test cluster: staging-serving-12 (A100-equivalent), edge-proxy image v3.11. Staging proxy has an internal buffer toggled via env PROXY_BUFFER_MS.
- Measurement harness: token-emission timestamping in SDK, plus tcpdump traces and server-side event traces (flush call times, write syscall times).
- We collected 10k streaming completions per config; reported p50/p95/p99 for per-token latency and end-to-end first-token latency.

Key observations (select):
1) Direct (no proxy), TCP_NODELAY=on, server flush immediate: p50=18ms p95=34ms p99=82ms (short tokens). Disabling NODELAY increased p95 from 34ms to 120ms and p99 to 320ms — classic Nagle/delayed-ACK behavior.
2) With edge-proxy (buffering enabled, PROXY_BUFFER_MS=30ms) and TCP_NODELAY=on, p99 jumped to 480ms even though direct cases were <100ms. The proxy was coalescing micro-writes to reduce network chatter.
3) gRPC/HTTP2 path had lower variance in some cases because frames were larger (multiplexing kept throughput higher), but when proxy was present and configured to re-chunk frames the behavior regressed and matched HTTP/1.1.
4) Grouped-2 flush (server buffers 2 tokens before flush) often gave best throughput but noticeable p99 spikes when combined with proxy buffering; grouped-4 made p99 dramatically worse.
5) Cold KV-cache runs added ~15–25ms per token on average; combined with proxy coalescing this hit p99 particularly badly for first-token latency (first-token p99 up to 700ms in worst configs).

Micro-trace example (short-token, proxy-buffering on, NODELAY on):
- t0: client opens stream, request headers 10ms
- t12ms: server emits token-1, write() syscalls small (22B) -> kernel pushes immediately (NODELAY)
- t13ms: proxy receives chunk, buffers until PROXY_BUFFER_MS=30ms -> delays forwarding
- t45ms: proxy flushes merged chunks -> client receives token-1 (first-token latency ~45ms)
- subsequent tokens see similar grouping -> tokens arrive in bursts rather than streaming cadence

Interpretation / what this means for us:
- Turning TCP_NODELAY on (runtime) is necessary but not sufficient in the presence of proxies that intentionally re-coalesce writes. If routing through edge proxies is common for hosted API, we need either (a) proxy-level sniffing/behavior changes or (b) an application-layer explicit flush marker that proxies honor (rare), or (c) an SDK-level coalescing strategy that writes larger logical chunks at the source to reduce proxy-induced batching unpredictability.
- For predictable p99 we need to consider the entire request path (client, proxy, runtime). Fixing only runtime socket flags leaves a blind spot.

Suggested mitigations to test next (priority ordered):
1) Proxy config change: add PROXY_HONOR_FLUSH=true so proxy forwards small DATA frames immediately (we can A/B in edge-proxy staging). Low-impact change to test.
2) Runtime: expose an optional "flush granularity" knob for streaming responses that batches into ~64B writes when system detects a proxied path (may increase token cost but stabilize p99).
3) SDK: adaptive coalescing — SDK starts with immediate flush for first 2 tokens then switches to grouped writes when telemetry shows no proxy buffering. This reduces cold-first-token regressions.
4) Telemetry: add a small marker that logs proxy-forward delays (server sees write->ack time and client sees receive times) to automatically detect re-coalescing on customer flows.

Action items (who/when):
- Priya: schedule a blocked A/B with edge-proxy team to enable PROXY_HONOR_FLUSH in a canary route (target: 2026-03-29).
- Ethan: prototype runtime flush-granularity knob (PR 4287) and add telemetry hooks for write timestamps (target: 2026-04-05).
- Sara: add SDK experiment for adaptive coalescing (node + python) and run 10k-run matrix (target: 2026-04-08).
- Marco: collect production sampling (non-PII) traces to find routes likely to experience this (target: 2026-03-26).

Open questions / risks:
- Some third-party proxies (cloud load balancers) cannot be reconfigured; how to handle those routes? Fallback options: conservative SDK coalescing or server-side larger chunking for known problematic egress IP ranges.
- Cost trade-offs: larger writes mean more bytes on wire because fewer TCP headers? (small effect) but might reduce multiplexing efficiency. Need to quantify token-cost delta.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could use an explicit HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE hack to force immediate flushes in proxies that mirror client WINDOW state — messy.
- For dedicated/private customers we can recommend network path config (set proxy passthrough) as part of onboarding docs; much easier than hunting in public edge.

Appendix - raw numbers (selected):
- Direct/NODELAY/on/immediate flush (short tokens): p50=18ms p95=34ms p99=82ms throughput=200 qps equivalent
- Direct/NODELAY/off/immediate flush: p50=20ms p95=120ms p99=320ms
- Proxy(buffer=30ms)/NODELAY/on/immediate flush: p50=24ms p95=112ms p99=480ms
- Proxy(buffer=30ms)/NODELAY/on/grouped-4: p50=80ms p95=240ms p99=700ms
- gRPC/proxy(buffer=30)/NODELAY/on: p50=30ms p95=140ms p99=540ms

If you care about reproducibility: see linked PR (runtime timestamps) and Jira ticket for the experimental harness. Will upload tcpdump snippets and flamegraphs to the ticket.

Tags for search: app-nagle, flush-cadence, proxy-coalesce, token-latency, staging-lab

End.
